newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 31.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The Reserve Bank of Australia yesterday cut its overnight cash rate by 50 basis points, reducing official interest rates to five percent. It is the fifth cut in official interest rates in the last 12 months and the RBA is confident the move will promote economic growth and job creation without increasing inflation. Page 1.

Davids Ltd chairman John David yesterday resigned from his position after he announced A$262.4 million in abnormal writedowns. The figures represent a possible 65 percent fall from 1996/97 earnings and the cancellation of the group's five cent dividend. Page 1.

The board of Telstra and its advisers on the company's planned A$10 billion public float are in conflict over profit forecasts in the forthcoming prospectus. The board has refused to issue the prospectus unless the float's global co-ordinators reduce their 1997/98 profit projections. Page 1.

Former Sex Discrimination Commissioner Sue Walpole has accused Attorney-General Daryl Williams of attempting to censor the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission through his plan to abolish the role of the Sex Discrimination Commissioner an other specialist human rights portfolios. Speaking at a Women, Management and Industrial Relations conference, Walpole said the government has sent a clear message to independent statutory bodies that they do not tolerate criticism. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Home buyers are set to benefit by an extra A$32 a month following the decision of the Reserve Bank yesterday to cut official interest rates by half a percentage point. Most lending agencies, however, have ignored the government's call to pass on the cut to small business loans. Page 1.

The Reserve Bank's decision yesterday to cut official interest rates will impact severely on the aged, with over half a million pensioners set to suffer a one percentage point cut in their interest earnings. The Commonwealth Bank, which holds A$7 billion in the special pensioner deeming accounts, yesterday called on the government to speed up its six-monthly review of the "deeming" interest rate. Page 1.

A UN Commission on Human Rights report presented to a meeting of indigenous leaders in Geneva claims that Australia's approach to land rights is marred with "discriminatory and colonial biases". The report also says the federal government's proposed amendments to the Native Title Act may result in extinguishing native title. Page 1.

The soon-to-be-released Goldsworthy report recommends the appointment of a market-access facilitator for the information and technology industries who would be responsible for identifying and combating trade barriers. The report claims that urgent action to promote the industries in Australia is needed if a forecast annual trade deficit of A$46 billion in the sector by 2005 is to be prevented. Page 2.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello has indicated that pensioners and retirees may have to accept a cut in interest rates on deeming accounts in order to get banks to pass on the full benefit of the latest official interest rate reduction. The federal government is responsible for setting the interest rates that banks pay on selected accounts for pensioners and retirees. Page 1.

Former Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser says he regrets approving the building of new Parliament House. Speaking at a Ethnic Communities Council of New South Wales meeting Fraser described the building as too big and too luxurious and said its annual budget of A$1.1 billion was a waste of money. Page 1.

Richard Basham, a member of the Police Commissioner's advisory group on criminal investigation and Sydney University's Anthropology Department head, has labelled as "woeful and pathetic" the level of resources available to police to combat Asian organised crime in Australia. Basham has blamed the low support police receive on a lack of political will. Page 3.

The New South Wales Teachers Federation and the Department of School Education yesterday reached agreement on how to report results from basic schools tests. Under the agreement individual results from students will not be published nor will schools be graded agains each other. However, parents will receive information on their child's performance and schools will have to issue an annual report which states broadly how their students compare to others across the state. Page 3.
THE AGE

Home loan interest rates are set to fall to a 30 year low following the Reserve Bank's decision yesterday to cut half a percentage point from official interest rates. Reductions in interest rates have slashed mortgage payments by up to A$316 a month in the past year with new standard home rates now being set at below seven percent. Page A1.

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello said yesterday that deeming interest rates will be reviewed following the Reserve Bank's cut in official interest rates. The Commonwealth Bank said yesterday that it was unable to pass on the full effect of the rate cut to homeowners while paying unrealistically high rates on deeming accounts. Page A1.

Victorian Transport Minister Robin Cooper has threatened to shut train lines if unions do not lift a work-to-rule ban which saw the stoppage of 85 trains yesterday. Cooper also stated that if the shutdown goes ahead hundreds of transport staff could be sood down without pay. Page A1.

The federal government is close to announcing an official date for the public float of one-third of Telstra, which could be valued at up to A$36 billion. A launch could be as early as the end of September, with November 13 being tipped as the date for the float's close. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
